title: Fiscal consolidations and productivity: Evidence from euro area regions
desc: With public debt high across Europe, how fiscal consolidations affect productivity is again a live question. This column studies spending-based consolidations in 139 euro area regions between 1999 and 2019, using a new utilisation-adjusted measure of total factor productivity. In regions more exposed to consolidation, output falls while measured productivity rises. The productivity gains arise almost entirely within sectors and coincide with a net decline in business establishments.

title: Explaining the stock market: Why is it still so hard?
desc: Physicists could already explain the motion of planets with extraordinary precision centuries ago. Finance still struggles to explain yesterday’s stock market movement. This column identifies a foundational failure of empirical asset pricing and makes significant progress towards explaining market movements using AI. Conventional measures account for remarkably little return variation, even with hindsight. Reasons extracted with AI from just one Wall Street Journal market recap per trading day explain about 30% of daily and 40% of monthly S&P 500 return variation out of sample.

title: The demographics of technology adoption and productivity growth
desc: Advanced economies are counting on artificial intelligence to revive productivity growth just as their workforces age. This column argues that the two trends are closely connected, because young workers adopt new technologies at far higher rates than old workers. Evidence from US local labour markets shows that younger workforces adopt more technology, see faster wage growth, and generate more innovation. title: Rent sharing under innovation tax breaks
desc: Governments use tax incentives to encourage innovation, but their benefits may extend beyond the firms claiming them. Using the Dutch innovation box and linked employer-employee data, this column shows that firms share part of their additional after-tax profits with incumbent workers, including those not directly engaged in R&D. Higher wages also coincide with lower job-to-job mobility among non-R&D workers. These findings highlight the labour market consequences of innovation policy.

title: EU economic outlook: Weathering the shock but eroding fiscal buffers
desc: Supported by the trade spillovers from the strong AI investment cycle, the European economy has weathered the prolonged energy shock better than feared. Yet, as this column describes, energy pressures and tighter financial conditions weigh on the outlook: growth should remain steady, while elevated inflationary pressures are set to broaden beyond energy, before eventually easing. Public finances are deteriorating, driven by rising interest and defence spending. Where debt is high and rising, governments need to exercise fiscal prudence.

title: Immigration and native welfare: The effect through wages and taxes
desc: Debates on immigration usually treat its labour market and fiscal effects separately. This column discusses the consequences of bringing them together in a model calibrated to 17 high-income countries. An inflow equal to 1% of the labour force, with the education mix of recent arrivals, raises native welfare in 14 of them. The sources of gains differ: non-college-educated natives gain mainly through higher earnings, college-educated natives mainly through lower labour taxes.

title: Emerging Europe’s defence industrial base: Between legacy firms and new entrants
desc: Defence budgets are rising across Europe, and several EBRD economies are leading the shift. Whether higher spending supports domestic industry depends on who can supply it. Drawing on the EBRD Transition Report 2026-27, this column shows that emerging Europe’s defence industry combines large, unproductive state-owned incumbents with young defence-tech startups that rarely advance beyond the earliest funding stage. Drones offer an opportunity, but the market for military drones is smaller than the one for commercial drones and supply chains depend heavily on China.

title: When transparency raises prices: Lessons from California’s all-in pricing law for short-term rentals
desc: Governments are cracking down on hidden fees, expecting all-in prices to sharpen competition and lower what consumers pay. This column studies California’s 2024 requirement that short-term rentals advertise fee-inclusive prices. Guests became more price-sensitive, yet prices rose by about 5%. Consumers still gained on average, largely because the market reshuffled: listings that depended on cleaning fees disproportionately left, higher-quality listings stayed, and cheaper entrants arrived.

desc: Proposals to shorten the workweek are back on the policy agenda in Europe and the US.
